title: Effects of Heat Stress and Sex on Pacing in Marathon Runners
authors: Trubee NW, Vanderburgh PM, Diestelkamp WS, Jackson KJ
journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
population: 22,990 men and 13,233 women at the 2007 and 2009 Chicago marathons (mean ambient temperature 26.67 C and 2.77 C), 5-km splits
findings: Pacing was the mean velocity of the last 12.2 km divided by that of the first 30 km.
Age, sex, heat stress and overall finish time were each simultaneous independent elements of pacing (p < 0.01).
Non-elite women paced better than non-elite men in both marathons, and the sex difference was larger in the warm race.
Elite men and women had better pacing than their non-elite counterparts, and no difference was found between elite men and women.
The authors advise coaches of novice runners to use a slower initial velocity in hotter temperatures to maintain or increase velocity later in the race.
limitations: Two races only (one hot, one cold), so heat stress is confounded with year and course conditions; temperature is the race mean, not a WBGT; the advice in the abstract is the authors' recommendation, not a tested intervention.
implications: In the warm Chicago race the late-race slowing of non-elite runners was greater, and heat was an independent element of pacing. Supports one line that heat raises the cost of a fast start; no figure.

verification.notes: Crossref matches (JSCR 28:1673-1678). Abstract read on Europe PMC. Crossref lists no correction, erratum or retraction notice (checked 2026-11-16).
